subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_description: Students examine objects they have brought to school and identify the materials each is made from. They record their findings in a two-column list, then share observations to discover that the same material can make many objects and one object can be made from several materials.

roles.role_description: Prompts students to look closely at everyday objects and introduces the term 'material' as any substance used to create an object.
Examines personal objects, lists them alongside their constituent materials, and shares observations with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter by holding up two or three classroom objects and asking what each is made from, establishing the word 'material'.
Each student examines objects on their desk, records a two-column list of object and material, and annotates any object made from more than one material.
Students share their lists aloud; the class builds a collective record on the board showing materials that appear more than once.
Teacher draws attention to the pattern: many objects, many materials, and some materials shared across very different objects.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit orients students to the chapter's central idea — that the physical world can be described and eventually classified by the materials objects are made from. Watch for students who conflate the object with its material (e.g., 'my bag is made of bag'); nudge them to name the actual substance. A quick check that every student has at least five distinct material names signals readiness to move on.
materials: Objects students carry to school (pencil, eraser, water bottle, bag, lunchbox, book)

periods.activity_description: Small groups receive a set of pictured objects and sort them into groups using any common property they choose — shape, colour, material, or use. Groups compare their schemes and notice that the same set of objects can be validly arranged in multiple ways, leading to a first encounter with the term classification.

roles.role_description: Circulates to prompt groups to articulate the property they used, and introduces the term 'classification' once groups share their schemes.
Sorts the pictured objects by a chosen common property, labels their grouping criterion, and explains their scheme to another group.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects this unit to the previous one: 'Last time we named materials; now we ask whether materials or objects can be arranged into groups.'
Each group sorts its set of pictured objects into groups using any property they choose and writes the grouping criterion at the top of their sheet.
Groups pair up, compare schemes, and discuss why two valid groupings of the same set can look different.
Teacher leads a brief whole-class share-out and formally introduces the term 'classification' and the idea that the purpose of the object influences which material is chosen for it.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established that many materials exist; this unit introduces the idea of organising them. A common error here is that students treat grouping as a single 'right answer' task — stress that any grouping backed by a consistent property is valid. If groups finish quickly, ask them to re-sort using a completely different property to deepen the discovery.
materials: Printed or drawn pictures of objects (book, key, glass tumbler, wooden ruler, rubber eraser, metal spoon, plastic bag, clay pot)
Scissors (optional, to cut and physically sort)
Grouping sheets with space for criterion label

periods.activity_title: Lustre, Hardness, and How We Test Them
periods.activity_description: Students examine a collection of material samples — metal pieces, rubber, wood scraps, paper, jute — first for lustre (shiny vs. not shiny) and then for hardness by pressing and scratching with a metal key. They record each material in a four-column table: material, lustrous or not, hard or soft, and what test they used.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the scratch test on one sample and clarifies that lustre is visible on freshly cut metal surfaces, cautioning that polished plastics can look shiny without being lustrous metals.
Tests each material sample for lustre and hardness, records results in the four-column table, and notes that hardness is relative (rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron).

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous one: 'We grouped objects; now we examine specific testable properties,' and demonstrates the scratch test on a metal piece and an eraser.
Groups test each material sample — pressing, scratching with a key, and observing surface appearance — and fill in the four-column table for all samples.
Groups share results; the class agrees on which materials are lustrous and which are hard, and discusses cases where a material's shine comes from polishing rather than lustre.
Teacher consolidates: lustrous materials are typically metals; hardness is relative, not absolute.

periods.teacher_notes: Students move from free classification in the previous unit to testing specific properties using defined procedures — a rise in cognitive demand. The most common misconception here is that anything shiny is a metal; direct attention to the plastic-coated or wax-polished samples to challenge this. Ask groups: 'Could rubber be both harder than one thing and softer than another at the same time?' to surface the relative nature of hardness.
materials: Small samples: iron nail, copper wire, aluminium foil, rubber band, wood scrap, paper strip, jute fibre

periods.activity_title: Light Through, Light Blocked, Light Blurred
periods.activity_description: Students place each of six objects — glass tumbler, butter paper, eraser, frosted glass, wooden board, window glass — between a torch and a white wall in a darkened corner. They record whether they can see the torch light clearly, partially, or not at all, then name each material transparent, translucent, or opaque and justify their label.

roles.role_description: Poses the inquiry question — 'Can all materials be seen through?' — and guides students to design their own one-sentence observation criterion before they test each object.
Tests each object with the torch, records what they observe about light passage, assigns the correct category label, and writes a one-sentence justification for each decision.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the inquiry question and connects it to the previous unit: 'We tested what a material looks like and how hard it is; now we ask what light does when it meets a material.'
Groups test each of the six objects in turn, recording their observations about light passage and assigning a category label with a written justification.
Groups compare their category assignments, resolve any disagreements (especially for frosted glass and butter paper), and arrive at class-wide agreed labels.
Teacher formalises the three terms — transparent, translucent, opaque — and asks students to name one more example of each from the room.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit continues the classification strand by adding a third testable property; the inquiry framing asks students to form criteria before testing, which is a step up from the guided testing in the previous unit. The most common confusion is placing frosted glass and butter paper in separate categories when students think 'a little blurry' and 'very blurry' are different — emphasise that translucent covers the whole range of partial transmission. A quick exit check: ask each student to hold up one object from their desk and call out its light-transmission category.
materials: Frosted glass pane or frosted plastic sheet
Window glass or clear plastic sheet
White wall or white paper screen

periods.activity_description: Students stir small, equal amounts of sugar, salt, chalk powder, sand, and sawdust separately into identical cups of water, observe what happens after stirring, and classify each substance as soluble or insoluble. They also observe that some liquids (cooking oil) form a separate layer in water, extending the solubility concept beyond solids.

roles.role_description: Introduces the terms 'soluble' and 'insoluble' after students have made their observations, and briefly mentions that dissolved gases like oxygen in water make aquatic life possible.
Measures equal amounts of each substance, stirs each into water, observes and records what happens, and classifies each as soluble or insoluble with a written observation note.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous two: 'We have classified materials by appearance and by how light travels through them; now we test how materials behave in water.'
Groups stir each substance into a separate cup of water, wait briefly, and record whether the substance disappears into the water, sinks but does not dissolve, or floats.

Groups share results and the class builds a soluble/insoluble table on the board; teacher introduces the terms and briefly notes that oil forms a separate layer, showing that liquids too can be insoluble in water.
Teacher highlights the ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) connection: salt and sugar dissolve in water, making ORS possible, showing a practical use of solubility.

periods.teacher_notes: Students have now tested three classification properties — lustre, transparency, and solubility — and this unit completes the observable-properties strand of the chapter before moving to measurable properties. Watch for the misconception that chalk powder 'dissolves' because it makes the water cloudy; help students see that cloudiness means particles are suspended, not dissolved — clarity (or absence of settled residue) is the marker. If a group finishes early, ask them to predict whether a fourth liquid (e.g., lemon juice) would mix with water or form a layer.
materials: 5 identical clear cups or glasses per group

periods.stage_label: Measure physical properties — mass and volume
periods.activity_title: Which Cup Is Heavier? Measuring Mass
periods.activity_description: Students fill three identical paper cups — one with water, one with sand, one with pebbles — predict which is heaviest, then use a simple balance to compare masses. They record predictions and measurements and articulate that equal-sized containers can have very different masses depending on what material fills them.

roles.role_description: Introduces mass as the measured property of 'how much matter is in something', distinguishes it from everyday use of 'weight', and explains how to read a simple balance.
Fills three cups, records predictions, measures with the balance, and writes a sentence explaining why the heaviest cup has more mass despite all cups being the same size.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the properties strand: 'We have sorted materials by what we see and how they behave; now we measure a property — mass — using an instrument.'
Students predict which cup will be heaviest, recording their prediction and reasoning before any measurement.
Groups use the balance to compare cups in pairs, then rank all three from lightest to heaviest, recording each comparison.
Groups share rankings and the class discusses why cups of the same size have different masses; teacher introduces grams and kilograms as standard units of mass.
Teacher previews the next unit: 'Mass tells us how much matter; volume tells us how much space — we explore that next.'

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the measurement strand and is the first time students use an instrument to quantify a material property rather than just classify it — a deliberate increase in demand. A common confusion is that the largest or fullest-looking container must be heaviest; the prediction step before measurement is important for surfacing and then challenging this idea. If a balance is unavailable, a simple improvised balance using a ruler balanced on a pencil and two identical containers works well.
materials: 3 identical paper or plastic cups per group

periods.stage_label: Measure physical properties — mass and volume
periods.activity_title: How Much Space Does It Take? Measuring Volume
periods.activity_description: Students compare two identical glass tumblers filled to different water levels and observe that the higher-filled tumbler contains more water occupying more space. They connect this to volume as the measure of space occupied by matter, read the volume markings on labelled bottles (1 L, 500 mL, 200 mL), and use a measuring jar to record volumes of water in millilitres.

roles.role_description: Poses the question 'Do both tumblers have the same amount of water?' and guides students to connect the observable difference in water level to the concept of volume, introducing litre and millilitre as units.
Observes the two tumblers, writes a sentence explaining the difference using the word 'volume', then reads and records volume markings from labelled bottles and a measuring jar.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous one: 'We measured mass; now we measure the space matter takes up — its volume.'
Teacher displays two identical tumblers with different water levels; students observe and write one sentence explaining the difference, using the word 'volume'.
Students examine labelled bottles and a measuring jar, read off volume values in litres and millilitres, and record them in a table.
Class discussion: students articulate that volume is the space a material occupies, and the teacher formalises the SI unit (cubic metre, m³) and the everyday units (L, mL) with correct notation.
Quick check: teacher asks students to state one thing about a material that mass tells us and one thing that volume tells us, setting up the final unit's synthesis.

periods.teacher_notes: Students come in having measured mass; this unit pairs volume with it to complete the measurable-properties strand before the final consolidation. A frequent confusion is that a taller container always holds more volume — use the identical-tumbler setup to make the comparison fair and direct attention to the water level, not the container shape. The distinction between litre as an everyday unit and cubic metre as the SI unit can be kept brief; the important takeaway is that volume, like mass, is measured with standard units.
materials: Labelled water bottles (1 L, 500 mL, 200 mL)
Measuring jar (or improvised measuring jar from a transparent bottle)

periods.stage_label: Define matter and apply the full property framework
periods.activity_title: Matter: The Property That Holds It All Together
periods.activity_description: Students revisit the full set of properties explored — lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility, mass, and volume — and determine which properties are universal (mass and volume) versus which are selective (only some materials have lustre or solubility). From this, they derive and record the definition of matter, then apply it to classify a new set of materials using the complete framework.

roles.role_description: Guides the class through a structured review table, asks which properties every material in the chapter had, and uses that reasoning to lead students to the definition of matter as anything with mass and volume.

Completes a review table for all materials studied, identifies the two universal properties, writes the definition of matter in their own words, and classifies three unfamiliar materials using the full framework.
Compares their classifications of the three unfamiliar materials, resolves disagreements by citing evidence from the property tests, and agrees on a final classification with justification.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a structured recall across all previous units: for each material studied, the class marks which properties apply in a shared board table.
Students individually examine the completed table and write one sentence identifying the two properties that every single material has.
Teacher formalises the definition of matter — anything that occupies space and has mass — and introduces the mass and volume SI units and notation conventions.
Groups classify three unfamiliar materials (e.g., air in a sealed balloon, cooking oil, a piece of cork) using the full property framework, citing evidence for each property claim.
Groups share their classifications; teacher draws connections to the earlier classification of living things, confirming that classifying non-living matter follows the same logic.

periods.teacher_notes: This final unit asks students to reason across the entire chapter — using every property studied to define matter and then apply that definition — which is the highest cognitive demand of the arc. A common error at this stage is writing 'matter is everything around us' instead of using mass and volume as the defining criteria; push students to justify why air in a balloon counts as matter (it has mass and occupies space). The unfamiliar-materials task in groups is the key assessment opportunity: listen for students who cite specific evidence ('the balloon gets heavier when inflated, so air has mass') rather than simply asserting a label.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for shared review table
Sealed balloon (inflated, to represent air as matter)
Optional: simple balance to demonstrate that an inflated balloon is heavier than a deflated one
homework: Choose any three objects at home that are made from more than one material. For each object, list its materials and write one sentence explaining why you think each material was chosen for that part of the object.
Find two labelled containers at home (e.g., a milk carton, a juice bottle). Write down the volume marked on each and explain in one sentence what that volume number tells you about the contents.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify and list materials objects are made from, then sort objects into groups by a chosen common property and encounter the term classification.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the material(s) an everyday object is made from and sort a given set of objects into groups by stating a consistent common property.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students test materials for lustre, hardness, light transmission, and solubility, recording results and assigning classification labels with justifications.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify a given material as lustrous or non-lustrous, hard or soft, transparent/translucent/opaque, and soluble or insoluble in water, citing the test or observation used for each classification.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Measure physical properties — mass and volume
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students measure mass using a balance and compare volumes using water levels and labelled containers, recording values in standard units.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can use a simple balance to compare masses and read volume from a measuring jar or labelled container, recording both in correct standard units (g/kg for mass; mL/L for volume).

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Define matter and apply the full property framework
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify mass and volume as universal properties of all materials, derive the definition of matter, and classify unfamiliar materials using the complete property framework.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why mass and volume define matter, write the definition of matter, and apply the full classification framework — lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility, mass, and volume — to classify and justify the categorisation of unfamiliar materials.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the material(s) an everyday object is made from and sort a given set of objects into groups by stating a consistent common property.

competency.competency_text: Classify matter based on observable physical characteristics including transparent, opaque, and translucent.

assessment_items.question_text: A student is asked to group the following four objects: an iron nail, a glass tumbler, an aluminium spoon, and a copper coin. Which grouping uses a single consistent property?

options.label: A
options.text: All four objects in one group because they are all hard materials.

options.label: B
options.text: Glass tumbler and copper coin in one group because both are shiny; iron nail and aluminium spoon in another group.

options.label: C
options.text: Iron nail, aluminium spoon, and copper coin in one group because they are all metals; glass tumbler in another group.

options.label: D
options.text: Iron nail and aluminium spoon in one group because they are used for eating; glass tumbler and copper coin in another group.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is grouping by use (function) rather than by a material property, indicating confusion between an object's purpose and what it is made of.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student overgeneralises — glass is typically hard too, so this grouping appears to use hardness but actually fails to distinguish materials from one another, indicating incomplete observation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student notices shine in copper but not in glass, or applies shine inconsistently; this reveals a surface-level observation without a consistently applied property criterion.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to read the question stem can be asked verbally: 'Which three of these objects are made from similar kinds of stuff?' Students who find the task easy can be asked to suggest a second valid grouping using a different property.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the material(s) an everyday object is made from and sort a given set of objects into groups by stating a consistent common property.

competency.competency_text: Classify matter based on observable physical characteristics including transparent, opaque, and translucent.

assessment_items.question_text: A water bottle has a plastic outer body, a rubber seal inside the cap, and a metal clip on the side. What does this tell us about the bottle?

options.label: A
options.text: Rubber and metal are not real materials because they are only small parts of the bottle.

options.label: B
options.text: The bottle is made from more than one material, with each material chosen for a specific part.

options.label: C
options.text: The bottle is made from plastic only, since that is what most of it is made from.

options.label: D
options.text: The bottle should be made entirely from one material to work properly.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student identifies only the dominant material and ignores other components, showing incomplete observation of an object's material composition.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student does not recognise that a material is a material regardless of how small a portion it forms — a misconception about what counts as a material.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student holds the misconception that objects are always made from a single material, which the chapter explicitly challenges through the concept that one object can use several materials.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be shown an actual water bottle and asked to point to each material before reading the question. Students who find the question straightforward can be asked to name a second real-world object that uses three or more different materials.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given material as lustrous or non-lustrous, hard or soft, transparent/translucent/opaque, and soluble or insoluble in water, citing the test or observation used for each classification.

competency.competency_text: Classify matter based on observable physical characteristics including transparent, opaque, and translucent.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Material | Appearance | Scratch test result | Water test result
Jute rope | Dull, rough | Scratches easily | Floats, does not dissolve
Aluminium foil | Shiny | Difficult to scratch | Does not dissolve
Chalk stick | Dull, white | Scratches easily | Turns water cloudy, settles
Cellophane sheet | Clear, glossy | Scratches with effort | Does not dissolve
assessment_items.question_text: A student tests four materials and records the results. Refer to the table provided. Which material is correctly described as lustrous AND hard?

options.label: A
options.text: Aluminium foil

options.label: B
options.text: Cellophane sheet

options.label: C
options.text: Chalk stick

options.label: D
options.text: Jute rope

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may focus on the physical nature of the rope without reading the scratch test result, indicating failure to use test evidence to classify hardness.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may recall that chalk is a well-known school material without applying the properties from the table — recall override of evidence-based classification.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may associate 'glossy' appearance with lustre and ignore the scratch test column — a confusion between surface polish/coating and true metallic lustre, which the chapter specifically cautions against.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find reading the table challenging can be supported by the teacher reading each row aloud. Students who answer correctly can be asked a follow-up: 'Is cellophane sheet lustrous? How do you know from the table?'

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given material as lustrous or non-lustrous, hard or soft, transparent/translucent/opaque, and soluble or insoluble in water, citing the test or observation used for each classification.

competency.competency_text: Classify matter based on observable physical characteristics including transparent, opaque, and translucent.

assessment_items.question_text: A student stirs chalk powder into water and notices the water turns cloudy, but after the mixture is left still, powder settles at the bottom. Which classification is correct for chalk powder in water, and what evidence supports it?

options.label: A
options.text: Insoluble — because chalk powder is white and white materials do not dissolve in water.

options.label: B
options.text: Insoluble — because the powder settled at the bottom rather than disappearing into the water.

options.label: C
options.text: Soluble — because it changed the colour of the water.

options.label: D
options.text: Soluble — because it mixed when stirred.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses a change in water appearance (cloudiness) with dissolving — a specific misconception the chapter addresses where suspended particles create cloudiness without true dissolution.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student treats the act of stirring as evidence of solubility rather than observing the outcome (whether the substance disappears) — procedural confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student uses colour as an invalid criterion for solubility, ignoring the settling observation — this indicates the student is applying an invented rule rather than reading the evidence.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can perform the chalk-and-water test physically before answering. For students who answer correctly, a follow-up question can ask: 'What would you observe differently if you stirred salt instead of chalk?'

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given material as lustrous or non-lustrous, hard or soft, transparent/translucent/opaque, and soluble or insoluble in water, citing the test or observation used for each classification.

competency.competency_text: Classify matter based on observable physical characteristics including transparent, opaque, and translucent.

assessment_items.question_text: A student is given three materials: a sheet of frosted glass, a strip of rubber, and a pinch of sugar. For each material, name one observable property test from the chapter and state what the result of that test would be.
expected_elements: Frosted glass — transparency test (hold up to light): objects can be seen through it but not clearly, so it is translucent.

Rubber — hardness test (press or scratch with a key): it can be compressed or scratched with effort but is harder than sponge, so it is soft relative to iron but hard relative to sponge (either comparative framing accepted).
Sugar — solubility test (stir into water): it disappears completely into the water, so it is soluble.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write full sentences can be offered a sentence frame: 'I tested __ by __. The result was __, so it is __.' Students who complete the task quickly can be asked to suggest a second valid test for one of the three materials.

assessment_items.stage_label: Measure physical properties — mass and volume
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can use a simple balance to compare masses and read volume from a measuring jar or labelled container, recording both in correct standard units (g/kg for mass; mL/L for volume).

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Cup | Filled with | Side of balance it rests on when compared to the other two
Cup P | Water | Middle (balanced against nothing alone)
Cup Q | Sand | Lower side when compared with Cup P
Cup R | Pebbles | Lower side when compared with Cup Q
assessment_items.question_text: Three identical cups are filled with water, sand, and pebbles. A student compares them on a balance and records the results. Refer to the table provided. Which cup has the greatest mass, and what does this tell the student?

options.label: A
options.text: All three cups have the same mass — because they are identical cups filled to the same level.

options.label: B
options.text: Cup P (water) — because water fills the cup completely with no air gaps.

options.label: C
options.text: Cup Q (sand) — because sand particles are heavier than individual water molecules.

options.label: D
options.text: Cup R (pebbles) — because it sits lower on the balance each time, meaning it has the greatest mass.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student uses a property of water (it fills with no air gaps) as a proxy for mass — confusing volume-filling behaviour with mass, a confusion between the two measurable properties.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reasons at the level of individual particles rather than reading the balance evidence — this shows the student is not yet using instrument data to reach a conclusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student over-applies the idea that identical containers hold the same amount — not distinguishing between the container (same) and its contents (different material, different mass).

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to read the comparative table can be walked through one row at a time by the teacher. Students who answer correctly can be asked: 'If you only had one measuring instrument — the balance — how would you rank all three cups from lightest to heaviest?'

assessment_items.stage_label: Measure physical properties — mass and volume
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can use a simple balance to compare masses and read volume from a measuring jar or labelled container, recording both in correct standard units (g/kg for mass; mL/L for volume).

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student reads two labels: Bottle X says '500 mL' and Bottle Y says '1 L'. The student says Bottle Y holds twice as much as Bottle X. Is the student correct, and which unit relationship supports the answer?

options.label: A
options.text: No — 1 L and 500 mL are different units and cannot be compared.

options.label: B
options.text: No — because litres measure mass and millilitres measure volume, so they describe different things.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — because 1 L equals 1000 mL, which is twice 500 mL.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — because a larger bottle always holds exactly twice the volume of a smaller bottle.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student knows the two unit names but has not grasped that they belong to the same measurement dimension and have a defined conversion, indicating incomplete unit understanding.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses mass and volume units — a direct confusion between the two measurable properties introduced in this stage, showing that the distinction has not yet been consolidated.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student reaches the correct conclusion but for the wrong reason — using a faulty generalisation about bottle size rather than the unit relationship, which would break down in any non-doubling example.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be shown two physical bottles with the labels to support reading. Students who answer correctly can be asked: 'If a third bottle holds 200 mL, how many of those bottles would you need to fill Bottle Y?'

assessment_items.stage_label: Measure physical properties — mass and volume
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can use a simple balance to compare masses and read volume from a measuring jar or labelled container, recording both in correct standard units (g/kg for mass; mL/L for volume).

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: Two identical boxes are placed on opposite sides of a balance. Box A contains a block of wood; Box B contains pebbles. Box B's side goes down. A student records: 'Box B is heavier.' Write two things the student should also record to make the measurement complete and scientifically useful.
expected_elements: The student should record the mass in a standard unit (grams or kilograms), not just state 'heavier' — a qualitative comparison must be expressed as a measured value to be scientifically useful.
The student should identify the instrument used (balance) and note that the comparison shows Box B has greater mass — distinguishing the instrument from the property it measures.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to identify what is missing can be prompted: 'If someone else wanted to repeat this measurement, what would they need to know that is not in the student's record?' Students who complete the task quickly can be asked to also state what happens to the balance if the two boxes have equal mass.

assessment_items.stage_label: Define matter and apply the full property framework
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why mass and volume define matter, write the definition of matter, and apply the full classification framework — lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility, mass, and volume — to classify and justify the categorisation of unfamiliar materials.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: A student claims: 'Sound is matter because it is everywhere around us and we can detect it.' Using the definition of matter from this chapter, which response best evaluates this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct — anything we can detect with our senses qualifies as matter.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is correct — sound occupies space because it spreads in all directions.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is incorrect — sound cannot be matter because it is invisible and not lustrous.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is incorrect — sound is not matter because it does not occupy space and has no mass; it is a form of energy that travels through matter.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not internalised the two-criteria definition of matter (mass and volume) and is using detectability as a proxy — a failure to apply the formal definition derived in the final unit.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student attempts to apply classification properties (lustre, visibility) instead of the defining properties of matter (mass and volume) — confusing classification criteria with the definition of matter itself.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student partially applies the volume criterion (spreading in all directions) but does not apply the mass criterion, showing incomplete use of the two-part definition.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the abstract scenario challenging can be guided by the teacher restating the definition: 'What two properties does everything that is matter have?' Students who answer correctly can be asked to evaluate a second case: 'Is light matter?'

assessment_items.stage_label: Define matter and apply the full property framework
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why mass and volume define matter, write the definition of matter, and apply the full classification framework — lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility, mass, and volume — to classify and justify the categorisation of unfamiliar materials.

competency.competency_text: Explain the importance of measurement and measure physical properties of matter in standard units using simple instruments.

assessment_items.question_text: Which pair of properties is shared by every material studied in this chapter — iron, rubber, sugar, water, air in a balloon, and wood — making those properties the basis for defining matter?

options.label: A
options.text: Hardness and solubility — because every material can be pressed and stirred in water to yield a result.

options.label: B
options.text: Lustre and hardness — because all materials have a surface that can be tested for shine and scratched.

options.label: C
options.text: Mass and volume — because every material takes up space and can be measured for how much matter it contains.

options.label: D
options.text: Solubility and transparency — because all materials either dissolve or do not dissolve, and either let light through or block it.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recalls lustre and hardness as prominent properties from the classification strand but has not identified them as selective rather than universal — failing to distinguish properties all matter has from properties only some matter has.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student selects two observable classification properties and applies flawed logic ('every material either dissolves or does not') — technically correct as a binary but missing the point that solubility and transparency do not define what matter is.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student applies the same flawed reasoning as above to hardness and solubility — selecting properties whose tests can be applied to anything rather than properties that are intrinsic to matter itself.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be asked to look back at their review table from the final unit and mark which properties had a result for every material. Students who answer correctly can be asked to explain in one sentence why lustre is not a defining property of matter.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why mass and volume define matter, write the definition of matter, and apply the full classification framework — lustre, hardness, transparency, solubility, mass, and volume — to classify and justify the categorisation of unfamiliar materials.

competency.competency_text: Classify matter based on observable physical characteristics including transparent, opaque, and translucent.

assessment_items.question_text: A student is given a new material — a block of paraffin wax. She says: 'I can classify it by lustre, hardness, and transparency, but not by solubility because I have not tested it yet. And I know it must have mass and volume because it is matter.' Evaluate her reasoning. Is each claim correct? Explain why or why not for each claim she makes.
look_for: Student correctly affirms that lustre, hardness, and transparency can be classified by observation or simple testing — and provides the correct likely result for wax (non-lustrous, relatively soft, opaque or translucent depending on thickness).

Student correctly affirms that solubility requires a test — wax is insoluble in water — and the student's reasoning that 'I have not tested it yet' shows appropriate epistemic caution consistent with scientific practice.
Student correctly affirms the mass-and-volume claim and connects it to the definition of matter, explaining that all matter has both properties regardless of its other characteristics.
Stronger responses explain WHY mass and volume are universal while lustre, hardness, transparency, and solubility are selective — linking back to the review table reasoning from the final unit.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing challenging can be supported with a sentence-starter frame: 'Her claim about lustre is __ because __ . Her claim about solubility is __ because __ . Her claim about mass and volume is __ because __.' Students who write strong responses can be asked to add one more unfamiliar material and predict its classification across all six properties.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Material | Lustrous or Non-lustrous | Hard or Soft | Transparent / Translucent / Opaque | Soluble or Insoluble in water | Has Mass? (Yes/No) | Has Volume? (Yes/No) | Is it Matter? (Yes/No)
Cork (stopper) | | | | | | |

assessment_items.task: Four materials are listed in the table provided. For each material: (1) complete every classification column using the properties you have tested in this chapter; (2) decide whether it has mass and volume; (3) state whether it is matter and give one sentence of evidence for your decision.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use each property in order: appearance (lustre), scratch test (hardness), light test (transparency), water test (solubility), balance reasoning (mass), space reasoning (volume). For the 'Is it matter?' column, apply the definition: matter is anything that occupies space and has mass.
format_of_output: Completed classification table with all columns filled
One sentence of evidence per material in the 'Is it Matter?' column

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's implied LO requires students to apply the complete property framework to unfamiliar materials and justify categorisation — a classification-with-justification task is the most direct demonstration vehicle for both the classification strand (C-1.1) and the measurement/matter-definition strand (C-1.3) simultaneously, satisfying the co_central requirement.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can apply the full observable-property classification framework, invoke the mass-and-volume definition of matter, and produce evidence-backed justifications — integrating both central competencies in a single reasoning act.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts students to work through properties in the order they were introduced across the chapter; this mirrors the arc of learning and helps students who are uncertain where to start. The teacher should treat the scaffold as optional support — students who fill the table without using it are showing independent integration of the framework.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly classify all four materials across all six properties, correctly identify all four as matter (including air in a balloon, which students may resist), and write evidence sentences that cite a specific observation or test result (e.g., 'The balloon got heavier when inflated, so air has mass'). Weak responses: leave mass and volume columns blank or write 'I don't know' for air, or write 'It is matter because it is a real thing' without citing mass or volume.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to reason about air in a balloon can be prompted: 'What happens to the balloon if you let the air out — does it feel the same in your hand?' Students who complete the task quickly can be asked to add a fifth row for a material of their own choosing and complete all columns independently.
